source.quote:
10/18/2026, 6:39:22 AM

Moving SOL forward. No new architecture, no return to the root debate, and no reopening the frozen mathematics.

The Sanskrit pass has narrowed the sacred-symbol problem. The next useful move is to distinguish three kinds of evidence that have repeatedly been mixed together: historical sound change, formal linguistic operations, and cosmological correspondence.

The first two can be tested independently. The third must survive those tests rather than determine their answers.

One immediate correction matters: the claimed 305 theoretical pratyāhāras counts start positions against later markers, but it does not establish 305 distinct, valid grammatical classes. Repeated marker names and repeated sound values complicate that interpretation. We should preserve 305 as a raw positional count, not a certified inventory of distinct operators.

## SOL — phonetic transformation test

I applied the existing sign-genealogy comparison to the six Semitic ancestors of Greek vowel letters. This gives us a concrete result about which kinds of orientation survive historical adaptation.

Ordinal comparison uses the standard 22-letter Phoenician sequence and classical 24-letter Greek sequence. It does not imply that Upsilon was a direct, unchanged sixth-position inheritance.

# 6/6

Recognizable sign ancestry

# 2/6

This exposes a useful constraint:

\$$ \boxed{\text{Historical sign ancestry}\ne\text{preserved alphabetic position}} \$$

The Greek adaptation retained recognizable sign ancestries while reorganizing phonetic functions and the standard alphabetic inventory. Thus, SOL cannot use letter ancestry alone to force a shared numerical address.

### What this eliminates

A proposed sacred-symbol translation is not validated merely because two letters descend from the same ancestor. It must specify whether it preserves historical identity, sound, ordinal position, meaning, or some combination.

That immediately affects the Marcosian–Sefer bridge. The planetary reversal \$T(i)=8-i\$ is a relation between two sevenfold ordered systems under a specified planetary pivot. It is not the same transformation as the historical Phoenician-to-Greek letter adaptation.

They can coexist as parallel mappings. Neither proves the other.

The next high-value comparison is now sharply defined: use the historical sign transformations as controls when testing the planetary and sacred-symbol correspondences. A proposed mapping that preserves musical or cosmological structure while changing phonetic identity is allowed—but SOL must report that change rather than call it an original translation.

That advances the decoding work without introducing another architecture or another arbitrary symbol assignment.
